strengths: Ambitious and timely problem: the paper targets multimodal, cross-domain, zero-shot time-series forecasting, including both deterministic and probabilistic settings.
The proposed system is reasonably comprehensive, combining text/image/time-series encoders, token distillation, modality-guided attention, and a flow-matching decoder with prototype initialization.
Evaluation covers several recognized benchmarks and compares against many recent foundation-model and supervised baselines, with generally strong reported results.
The paper includes useful ablations for the two main architectural ideas and reports basic efficiency statistics.
weaknesses: The central multimodal evidence is weakened by possible target leakage: the generated textual descriptions are produced from raw time-series segments and explicitly ask GPT-4 to analyze the future trend. It is unclear whether test-time text contains only information available at the forecast origin.

The multimodal corpus is largely synthetic and under-specified. The paper gives only one prompt example, no systematic quality control, no release plan, and limited analysis of how generated text affects generalization versus memorizing prompt artifacts.

Reproducibility is limited: no Aurora code or pretrained model is provided, pretraining takes about 30 days on 8 A800 GPUs, and many implementation details for baseline adaptation, generation steps, and text/image preprocessing remain underspecified.

The comparison protocol is not fully convincing. Some baselines have missing entries or excluded datasets, while aggregate claims rely on uneven coverage; the few-shot versus full-shot comparison is not clearly apples-to-apples given Aurora's large external pretraining.

Ablations are too coarse for the number of proposed components. There is no clean decomposition of text vs image contributions, synthetic text quality, prototype-bank initialization, number of flow steps, modality masking, or calibration/sharpness of probabilistic forecasts.

Novelty is incremental at the component level: many pieces are borrowed from existing multimodal transformers, time-series-to-image methods, and flow matching; the main novelty is their combination rather than a clearly new principle.

weaknesses: The central evaluation is potentially compromised by label leakage: the appendix prompt asks GPT-4 to analyze the future trend and characteristics of a time-series segment, so the text modality may encode target information. The paper does not clearly rule this out for pretraining or evaluation descriptions.

Reproducibility is weak: the method depends on a large GPT-4-generated corpus, a 418.6M-parameter model trained for about 30 days on 8 A800 GPUs, but provides no code, checkpoints, generated text data, seeds, or sufficiently detailed generation and training recipes.

Comparison fairness is not fully convincing. Aurora receives massive multimodal pretraining, while several baselines are evaluated under different pretraining/data-availability conditions; many table entries are missing or excluded, and there is no statistical testing.

The method is under-specified in important places, including whether BERT/ViT are frozen or trained, how missing modalities are handled, how the guided-attention correlation term is scaled, how multivariate series interact under channel independence, and how prototype retrieval behaves.

Ablations are too limited for the strength of the claims: there are no text-only/image-only studies, corpus-size studies, synthetic-text quality controls, prototype-bank-size or flow-step analyses, or probabilistic calibration/coverage evaluation.

The paper has many clarity and polish issues, including repeated typos, awkward claims, tiny dense tables, inconsistent metric wording, duplicated or weakly relevant references, and overstatements such as claiming best performance despite several cases where Aurora is not best.
